---
title: "TD, PD and FD on one scale"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(bg = "white"), collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", dpi = 150)
```

tidydiversity measures three dimensions of diversity with the same Hill
number framework:

* **Taxonomic diversity (TD)** treats every species as equally distinct.
* **Phylogenetic diversity (PD)** weights species by the branch lengths of
  a phylogeny (Chao, Chiu and Jost 2010, 2014).
* **Functional diversity (FD)** weights species by their trait distances,
  using the attribute-diversity approach of Chao et al. (2019).

Each is an effective number of species of order `q`, so the three can be
plotted on the same axis. Every dimension works with abundance data
(individuals) and with incidence data (detections in sampling units such
as traps, baits or survey days), with bootstrap standard errors and
confidence intervals throughout. The estimators reproduce
[iNEXT.3D](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=iNEXT.3D) and this is checked
in the package test suite.

## The concept

Counting species treats every species as equally different from every
other. But a site with ten species of one genus is less diverse, in an
evolutionary sense, than a site with ten species from ten families; and a
site where all trees are shade-tolerant and slow-growing is less diverse
in function than one with a mix of strategies. The three dimensions
answer different questions:

| Dimension | Question | Unit of the result |
|---|---|---|
| **TD** | How many species? | Effective number of species |
| **PD** | How much evolutionary history? | Effective number of equally distinct lineages (with `pd_unit = "mean"`) |
| **FD** | How many distinct ecological roles? | Effective number of functionally distinct species |

Because all three are Hill numbers, they share the same orders `q` and
the same rarefaction and coverage methods, and the patterns can be
compared directly. **Disagreement between dimensions is the interesting
result**: a site rich in species but poor in function holds many
redundant species, which may buffer it against losses (insurance) but
also means few distinct roles.

## Data

The example uses the Brazilian rainforest tree data shipped with iNEXT.3D:
abundances at two sites (`Edge` and `Interior`), a time-calibrated
phylogeny and a Gower distance matrix of traits.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(tidydiversity)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data(list = c(
  "Brazil_rainforest_abun_data", "Brazil_rainforest_phylo_tree",
  "Brazil_rainforest_distance_matrix"
), package = "iNEXT.3D")
wide <- Brazil_rainforest_abun_data
brazil <- tibble(
  site = rep(colnames(wide), each = nrow(wide)),
  species = rep(rownames(wide), ncol(wide)),
  n = unlist(wide, use.names = FALSE)
) |>
  filter(n > 0)
tree <- Brazil_rainforest_phylo_tree
traits <- as.matrix(Brazil_rainforest_distance_matrix)
```

## Observed and asymptotic diversity {.tabset}

### TD

```{r}
set.seed(1)
div_estimate(brazil, abundance = n, nboot = 50)
```

**How to read it.** `observed` is the sample value and `estimate` the
asymptotic value (what a complete census would give). The Interior holds
more species (514 estimated against 445), but at q = 2, which counts
only dominant species, the Edge is higher (86 against 75): the Interior
has more rare species, the Edge a more even set of common ones.

### PD

`reftime` defaults to the age of the root of the tree pruned to the observed
species. With `pd_unit = "mean"` (the default) PD is divided by `reftime`,
giving the effective number of lineages.

```{r}
div_estimate(brazil, abundance = n, type = "PD", tree = tree, nboot = 50)
```

**How to read it.** PD of order 0 is the total branch length divided by
the reference time (400 million years here), so 80 means the Edge's
species span as much evolutionary history as 80 lineages each 400 Myr
long. The Interior has more evolutionary history at every order, in line
with its higher richness.

### FD

`tau` defaults to the mean distance between two individuals in the pooled
data. Species closer than `tau` count as functionally identical.

```{r}
div_estimate(brazil, abundance = n, type = "FD", distance = traits, nboot = 50)
```

**How to read it.** FD is small (6-7) compared with TD (hundreds)
because most tree species are functionally similar: with species closer
than `tau` = 0.35 counted as one, the hundreds of species collapse into
about six or seven functional groups. **Here the Edge is more diverse
than the Interior at every order**, the opposite of richness: edge
conditions (light, wind, disturbance) favour a wider range of strategies,
whereas the Interior's extra species are functionally redundant.

### FD (area under the tau profile)

`tau = "auc"` integrates FD over every threshold from 0 to 1, so no single
threshold has to be chosen.

```{r}
div_estimate(brazil,
  abundance = n, type = "FD", distance = traits, tau = "auc",
  nboot = 20
)
```

The area under the tau profile gives the same conclusion without having
to choose a threshold, which makes it the more robust choice to report.

## Standardised comparison

`type = "all"` (or several types, such as `c("TD", "PD")`) analyses the
dimensions together and returns one tibble with a `type` column.

Standardise every dimension to the same sample coverage. Coverage is
computed from the species counts, as in iNEXT.3D, and the PD and FD values
are then evaluated at the matching sample size.

```{r}
std <- div_standardise(brazil,
  abundance = n, type = "all", tree = tree, distance = traits,
  coverage = 0.97, nboot = 0
)
std |> select(type, site, q, m, coverage, diversity)
```

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Diversity profiles at 97 percent coverage for TD, PD and FD at two sites."}
ggplot(std, aes(q, diversity, colour = site)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_tidydiversity() +
  labs(y = "Effective number of species", colour = NULL) +
  theme_tidydiversity()
```

**Interpretation.** All three curves flatten within the 36 samples of
each period: the monthly survey was effectively complete for q = 1. The
two periods overlap in every dimension (for example TD 30.1 and 31.5
effective species, with overlapping intervals), so fish diversity did
not change between 2013-2015 and 2016-2018.


**Interpretation.** At equal coverage (97%), the profiles show the
contrast at a glance: in PD the Interior lies above the Edge at every
q, in TD it does except for the dominant species (q = 2), while in FD the Edge lies above the
Interior at every q. A forest interior with more species is not
necessarily the one with the most ecological roles.

## Incidence data

Many surveys record which species were detected in each sampling unit
rather than how many individuals were counted. Give the unit column with
`unit`; each site is then described by the number of units in which each
species was found and the number of units sampled, and every estimate is
incidence-based (Chao et al. 2014). The same `type`, `tree` and `distance`
arguments give incidence-based PD and FD. For PD a branch is present in a
unit when any species below it was detected there.

The example uses the fish survey shipped with iNEXT.3D: monthly samples in
two periods (2013-2015 and 2016-2018, 36 samples each) with a phylogeny and
a trait distance matrix. The results reproduce iNEXT.3D, and this is
checked in the test suite.

```{r fish}
data(list = c(
  "Fish_incidence_data", "Fish_phylo_tree", "Fish_distance_matrix"
), package = "iNEXT.3D")
fish <- bind_rows(lapply(names(Fish_incidence_data), function(period) {
  m <- Fish_incidence_data[[period]]
  hit <- which(m > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
  tibble(
    site = period, species = rownames(m)[hit[, 1]],
    sample = colnames(m)[hit[, 2]], n_samples = ncol(m)
  )
}))
fish
```

```{r fish-3d, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Incidence-based rarefaction and extrapolation of TD, PD and FD for two periods of a fish survey."}
set.seed(1)
fish_curves <- div_rarefy(fish,
  unit = sample, n_units = n_samples, q = 1, type = "all",
  tree = Fish_phylo_tree, distance = as.matrix(Fish_distance_matrix),
  knots = 20, nboot = 30
)
ggplot(fish_curves, aes(m, diversity, colour = site, fill = site)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = method == "extrapolation")) +
  geom_point(data = filter(fish_curves, method == "observed"), size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_tidydiversity() +
  scale_fill_tidydiversity() +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of samples", y = "Diversity of order q = 1",
    colour = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tidydiversity()
```

The ant baits in `png_ants` are incidence data too: each bait is a
sampling unit, and `baits` gives the 60 baits set at every elevation and
season, including those no ant visited. Incidence-based (Chao2) richness:

```{r ants-incidence}
set.seed(1)
div_estimate(png_ants,
  unit = bait, n_units = baits, q = 0, .by = season, nboot = 50
)
```

These incidence-based estimates agree closely with the abundance-type
estimates in [Alpha diversity and rarefaction](alpha-rarefaction.html),
including the very uncertain value at 700 m in the dry season.

## How to report it

> Taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional diversity (Hill numbers of
> orders 0-2; Chao et al. 2014, 2019) were estimated with tidydiversity
> and compared at 97% sample coverage. Functional diversity was computed
> from Gower trait distances, integrating over all thresholds (area under
> the tau profile). The Interior had higher taxonomic and phylogenetic
> diversity, but the Edge had higher functional diversity at every order
> of q.

Name the tree (and its time unit), the trait distance, the threshold
`tau` or AUC, and the coverage level.


## References

Chao, A., Chiu, C.-H. and Jost, L. (2014). Unifying species diversity,
phylogenetic diversity, functional diversity, and related similarity and
differentiation measures through Hill numbers. *Annual Review of Ecology,
Evolution, and Systematics*, 45, 297-324.
<https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-ecolsys-120213-091540>

Chao, A., Chiu, C.-H., Villeger, S. et al. (2019). An attribute-diversity
approach to functional diversity, functional beta diversity, and related
(dis)similarity measures. *Ecological Monographs*, 89, e01343.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1343>

Chao, A., Gotelli, N. J., Hsieh, T. C., Sander, E. L., Ma, K. H., Colwell,
R. K. and Ellison, A. M. (2014). Rarefaction and extrapolation with Hill
numbers: a framework for sampling and estimation in species diversity
studies. *Ecological Monographs*, 84, 45-67.
<https://doi.org/10.1890/13-0133.1>
